question: How far can the danger zone extend from the front bumper of a school bus, and which part of that area is most dangerous?
choice_a: The danger zone does not extend in front of the bus
choice_b: As much as 30 feet, with the first 10 feet being the most dangerous
choice_c: As much as 100 feet, uniformly dangerous throughout
choice_d: As much as 5 feet, with the last foot being most dangerous
explanation: The danger zone may extend as much as 30 feet from the front bumper of the school bus, with the first 10 feet being the most dangerous.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.1.1, Danger Zones

question: Why is the area to the left of a school bus always considered dangerous?
choice_a: There is no special danger to the left side
choice_b: Because of passing cars
choice_c: Because the driver cannot see it at all
choice_d: Because it is closest to the fuel tank
explanation: The area to the left of the bus is always considered dangerous because of passing cars.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.1.1, Danger Zones

question: How far behind a school bus can the blind spot extend, depending on the length and width of the bus?
choice_a: Up to 10 feet
choice_b: There is no blind spot behind a school bus
choice_c: Up to 50 feet
choice_d: Up to 400 feet
explanation: The blind spot behind the bus extends 50 to 150 feet and could extend up to 400 feet depending on the length and width of the bus.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.1.3, Outside Left and Right Side Flat Mirrors

question: When properly adjusted, how far behind the bus should the outside left and right side flat mirrors allow the driver to see?
choice_a: 1,000 feet
choice_b: 200 feet or 4 bus lengths behind the bus
choice_c: Flat mirrors are not used to view behind the bus
choice_d: 20 feet or 1 bus length
explanation: Properly adjusted flat mirrors should let the driver see 200 feet or 4 bus lengths behind the bus, along the sides of the bus, and the rear tires touching the ground.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.1.3, Outside Left and Right Side Flat Mirrors

question: What is a known characteristic of the outside left and right side convex mirrors on a school bus?
choice_a: They present a view of people and objects that does not accurately reflect their size and distance from the bus
choice_b: They provide a perfectly accurate depiction of distance
choice_c: They are used only for checking tire pressure visually
choice_d: They are mounted on the roof of the bus
explanation: Convex mirrors provide a wide-angle view of traffic, clearances, and students at the side of the bus, but present a view of people and objects that does not accurately reflect their size and distance from the bus.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.1.4, Outside Left and Right Side Convex Mirrors

question: What is the purpose of the outside left and right side crossover mirrors on a school bus?
choice_a: To monitor engine temperature
choice_b: To see the front bumper 'danger zone' area directly in front of the bus that is not visible by direct vision
choice_c: To check tire tread depth remotely
choice_d: To replace the need for the overhead inside rearview mirror
explanation: Crossover mirrors are used to see the front bumper 'danger zone' area directly in front of the bus that is not visible by direct vision, and to view the danger zone to the left side and right side of the bus.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.1.5, Outside Left and Right Side Crossover Mirrors

question: What should be visible in the top of the overhead inside rearview mirror when it is properly positioned?
choice_a: The front bumper
choice_b: The top of the rear window
choice_c: Only the driver's own reflection
choice_d: The bus's exhaust pipe
explanation: The overhead inside rearview mirror should be positioned to see the top of the rear window in the top of the mirror, and all of the students, including the heads of the students right behind the driver.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.1.6, Overhead Inside Rearview Mirror

question: According to the manual, are more students killed while getting on or off a school bus, or while riding as passengers inside?
choice_a: More students are killed as passengers inside the bus
choice_b: More students are killed while getting on or off the bus than as passengers inside
choice_c: Fatalities are roughly equal between the two situations
choice_d: The manual does not address this comparison
explanation: More students are killed while getting on or off a school bus each year than are killed as passengers inside a school bus, which is why loading/unloading procedures are critical.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.2, Loading and Unloading

question: May a school bus driver change the location of a bus stop on their own judgment?
choice_a: No, the location should never be changed without written approval from the appropriate school district official
choice_b: Yes, at any time the driver believes it is safer
choice_c: Only the students may request a stop change
choice_d: Yes, but only during winter weather
explanation: A driver should never change the location of a bus stop without written approval from the appropriate school district official.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.2.1, Approaching the Stop

question: When approaching a school bus stop, approximately how far before the stop should the alternating flashing amber warning lights be activated (if so equipped)?
choice_a: At least 200 feet, or approximately 5-10 seconds before the stop
choice_b: Only after coming to a complete stop
choice_c: At least 1,000 feet
choice_d: Amber lights are activated only after the red lights
explanation: The driver should activate alternating flashing amber warning lights at least 200 feet or approximately 5-10 seconds before the school bus stop, or in accordance with state law.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.2.1, Approaching the Stop

question: When stopping to load students, how far away from the students at the designated stop should the front bumper of the bus be, and why?
choice_a: At least 10 feet away, forcing the students to walk to the bus so the driver has a better view of their movements
choice_b: 50 feet away, with students transported by an aide
choice_c: There is no specific distance requirement
choice_d: Right up against the students to save time
explanation: The driver should bring the school bus to a full stop with the front bumper at least 10 feet away from students at the designated stop, forcing the students to walk to the bus so the driver has a better view of their movements.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.2.1, Approaching the Stop

question: During loading, when should students board the school bus?
choice_a: As soon as the bus comes to a stop, without waiting for a signal
choice_b: Only after the driver exits the bus
choice_c: Whenever the amber lights are flashing
choice_d: Only when signaled by the driver
explanation: Students should board the bus only when signaled by the driver, after waiting in a designated location facing the bus as it approaches.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.2.2, Loading Procedures

question: During unloading procedures on the route, why should the driver count the number of students while unloading?
choice_a: Counting is not part of the unloading procedure
choice_b: To confirm the location of all students before pulling away from the stop
choice_c: It is only necessary at the final stop of the route
choice_d: To report ridership numbers to the school district daily
explanation: During unloading, the driver should count the number of students while unloading to confirm the location of all students before pulling away from the stop.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.2.3, Unloading Procedures on the Route

question: If a driver has missed a student's unloading stop, what should the driver NOT do?
choice_a: Radio the dispatcher
choice_b: Continue the route
choice_c: Back up
choice_d: Stop at the next safe location
explanation: If a driver has missed a student's unloading stop, the driver should not back up, and should follow local procedures instead.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.2.3, Unloading Procedures on the Route

question: When students must cross the roadway after exiting the bus, how far in front of the bus should they walk before crossing, and how far from the side of the bus?
choice_a: At least 50 feet in front of the bus
choice_b: Directly along the side of the bus without stepping away
choice_c: At least 10 feet away from the side of the bus, to a location at least 10 feet in front of the right corner of the bumper
choice_d: There is no specified distance for crossing procedures
explanation: Students crossing the roadway should walk approximately 10 feet away from the side of the school bus, to a location at least 10 feet in front of the right corner of the bumper, while remaining away from the front of the bus.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.2.3, Additional Procedures for Students That Must Cross the Roadway

question: What should students do if they drop an object near the bus during loading or unloading?
choice_a: Wait for the bus to leave, then retrieve it
choice_b: Immediately pick it up before boarding
choice_c: Leave the dropped object, move to a point of safety, and try to get the driver's attention to retrieve it
choice_d: Ask another student to retrieve it
explanation: Students should be told to leave any dropped object and move to a point of safety out of the danger zones, then attempt to get the driver's attention to retrieve the object -- stopping to pick it up can cause the student to disappear from the driver's sight at a dangerous moment.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.2.5, Special Dangers of Loading and Unloading, Dropped or Forgotten Objects

question: What should a school bus driver look for during a post-trip inspection walking through and around the bus?
choice_a: Articles left on the bus, sleeping students, open windows and doors, and mechanical/operational problems
choice_b: Only tire pressure
choice_c: Post-trip inspections are not required for school buses
choice_d: Only fuel level
explanation: The post-trip inspection includes looking for articles left on the bus, sleeping students, open windows and doors, mechanical/operational problems (with special attention to mirror systems, flashing warning lamps, and stop signal arms), and damage or vandalism.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.2.6, Post-trip Inspection

question: As a general rule, is it usually safer to keep students on the bus or evacuate them during an emergency, if it does not expose them to unnecessary risk?
choice_a: Student safety and control is usually best maintained by keeping students on the bus during an emergency
choice_b: Students should always be evacuated immediately in any emergency
choice_c: There is no general guidance on this decision
choice_d: The decision should always be made by the students themselves
explanation: As a general rule, student safety and control is best maintained by keeping students on the bus during an emergency and/or impending crisis situation, if doing so does not expose them to unnecessary risk or injury.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.3.1, Planning for Emergencies

question: How far off the road, in the direction of oncoming traffic, should a safe evacuation place generally be located?
choice_a: At least 10 feet
choice_b: Distance from the road is not a factor
choice_c: At least 100 feet
choice_d: At least 1,000 feet
explanation: A safe place will be at least 100 feet off the road in the direction of oncoming traffic, to keep students from being hit by debris if another vehicle collides with the bus.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.3.2, Evacuation Procedures

question: How far upwind should students be led during an evacuation if there is a risk from spilled hazardous materials?
choice_a: Upwind distance does not matter for hazmat spills
choice_b: At least 300 feet
choice_c: At least 1 mile
choice_d: At least 20 feet
explanation: Students should be led upwind of the bus at least 300 feet if there is a risk from spilled hazardous materials.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.3.2, Evacuation Procedures

question: Under which of the following conditions must a driver evacuate the bus?
choice_a: Evacuation is never mandatory; it is always the driver's discretion
choice_b: Only when all students agree it is necessary
choice_c: Only when a school administrator gives explicit permission
choice_d: The bus is on fire or there is a threat of fire, or the bus is stalled on or adjacent to a railroad-highway crossing
explanation: Mandatory evacuation conditions include the bus being on fire or threatened by fire, being stalled on or adjacent to a railroad-highway crossing, the position of the bus changing to increase danger, imminent danger of collision, or a need to quickly evacuate because of a hazardous materials spill.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.3.1, Mandatory Evacuations

question: If a bus stalls or is trapped on railroad tracks, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Get everyone out and off the tracks immediately, moving away from the tracks and toward the train
choice_b: Wait inside the bus for the train to stop
choice_c: Attempt to restart the bus for up to five minutes before evacuating
choice_d: Move everyone away from the tracks and away from the train
explanation: If a bus stalls or is trapped on the tracks, the driver must get everyone out and off the tracks immediately, moving everyone far from the bus at an angle that is both away from the tracks and toward the train.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.4.4, Bus Stalls or Trapped on Tracks

question: What is a 'passive' railroad-highway crossing?
choice_a: A crossing that is permanently closed to bus traffic
choice_b: A crossing equipped with flashing lights and gates
choice_c: A crossing that does not have any type of traffic control device, requiring the driver to decide if it is safe to cross
choice_d: A crossing only found on interstate highways
explanation: A passive crossing does not have any type of traffic control device; the decision to proceed rests entirely with the driver, who must recognize the crossing, search for a train, and decide if there is sufficient clear space to cross safely.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.4.1, Types of Crossings

question: At an active railroad-highway crossing with gates, when should a driver stop, and what should they do if the gate stays down after the train passes?
choice_a: Stop only after the gate has fully lowered
choice_b: Drive around a stuck gate immediately after the train passes
choice_c: Stop when the lights begin to flash and before the gate lowers; if the gate stays down after the train passes, call the dispatcher rather than driving around it
choice_d: Gates require no special stopping procedure
explanation: A driver should stop when the lights begin to flash and before the gate lowers across the road lane, remaining stopped until the gates go up and lights stop flashing; if the gate stays down after the train passes, the driver should call the dispatcher instead of driving around the gate.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.4.2, Warning Signs and Devices, Gates

question: When approaching a railroad crossing, at what distance should a school bus stop from the nearest rail for the best view of the tracks?
choice_a: Exactly at the cross-buck sign, regardless of distance
choice_b: No closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet
choice_c: There is no minimum or maximum distance
choice_d: At least 200 feet
explanation: At the crossing, the driver should stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail, where they have the best view of the tracks.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.4.3, Recommended Procedures, At the Crossing

question: At a multiple-track crossing, where should a school bus stop, and when should it proceed?
choice_a: The bus should never cross multiple-track crossings
choice_b: Stop only before the first set of tracks, and proceed across all tracks only once sure no train is approaching on any track
choice_c: Stop between each set of tracks individually
choice_d: It is unnecessary to stop for the second and later tracks
explanation: At a multiple-track crossing, the driver should stop only before the first set of tracks, and when sure no train is approaching on any track, proceed across all of the tracks until completely clear of them.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.4.3, Recommended Procedures, Crossing the Track

question: As a general rule, how much should a driver add to the length of the school bus to determine an acceptable containment or storage area on the far side of a crossing?
choice_a: 15 feet
choice_b: No additional distance is needed beyond the bus length
choice_c: 2 feet
choice_d: 50 feet
explanation: As a general rule, a driver should add 15 feet to the length of the school bus to determine an acceptable amount of containment or storage area needed to completely clear the tracks on the other side.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.4.4, Containment or Storage Areas

question: If there is a behavior problem on the bus while students are unloading, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Ignore the problem until the end of the route
choice_b: Wait until the students unloading are safely off the bus and have moved away before dealing with the problem
choice_c: Radio the school administrator before continuing the loading process
choice_d: Immediately stop unloading to address the problem
explanation: Loading and unloading requires all of the driver's concentration; if there is a behavior problem, the driver should wait until the students unloading are safely off the bus and have moved away, pulling over if necessary to handle the problem.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.5.1, Don't Deal with On-bus Problems When Loading and Unloading

question: May a driver put a student off the bus anywhere other than at school or the student's designated bus stop?
choice_a: Yes, at any location the driver deems appropriate
choice_b: Only if the student requests it
choice_c: No, a student should never be put off the bus except at school or at their designated school bus stop
choice_d: Yes, but only with the student's parent's prior verbal consent given that day
explanation: A driver should never put a student off the bus except at school or at their designated school bus stop; if an offense is too serious to safely continue, the driver should call for a school administrator or police.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.5.2, Handling Serious Problems

question: The Department of Transportation requires antilock braking systems on air-braked trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies built on or after what date?
choice_a: March 1, 1999
choice_b: July 1, 1995
choice_c: January 1, 2000
choice_d: March 1, 1998
explanation: The DOT requires antilock braking systems on air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies) built on or after March 1, 1998.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.6.1, Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: The Department of Transportation requires antilock braking systems on hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a GVWR of 10,000 lbs or more built on or after what date?
choice_a: January 1, 2005
choice_b: March 1, 1998
choice_c: March 1, 1999
choice_d: Hydraulically braked buses are exempt from ABS requirements
explanation: Hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a gross vehicle weight rating of 10,000 lbs or more built on or after March 1, 1999, are required to have ABS.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.6.1, Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: In emergency braking on a school bus equipped with ABS, should the driver pump the brakes?
choice_a: Yes, pumping the brakes is always recommended with ABS
choice_b: Pumping is required only above 40 mph
choice_c: No, do not pump the brakes on a bus with ABS during emergency braking
choice_d: It makes no difference whether the brakes are pumped
explanation: Regardless of whether the bus has ABS, the driver should brake the same way, but in emergency braking, the driver should not pump the brakes on a bus with ABS.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.6.3, Braking with ABS

question: If the yellow ABS malfunction lamp stays on after the bulb check or comes on while driving, what does this indicate?
choice_a: The driver may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels, but still has regular brakes and should get the system serviced soon
choice_b: The lamp is malfunctioning and can be ignored
choice_c: The entire braking system, including regular brakes, has failed
choice_d: The bus must be evacuated immediately
explanation: If the ABS malfunction lamp stays on after the bulb check or comes on while driving, the driver may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels; the driver still has regular brakes and should drive normally, but get the system serviced soon.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.6.4, Braking if ABS is Not Working

question: Which statement correctly describes a limitation of ABS?
choice_a: ABS guarantees a shorter stopping distance in all conditions
choice_b: ABS will not necessarily shorten stopping distance, though it helps maintain vehicle control
choice_c: ABS allows a driver to safely follow more closely
choice_d: ABS compensates for poor brake maintenance
explanation: ABS won't necessarily shorten stopping distance -- it helps maintain vehicle control, but it won't allow faster driving, closer following, or compensate for bad brakes or poor maintenance.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.6.5, Safety Reminders

question: How much tail swing can a school bus have during turning movements?
choice_a: Up to ten feet
choice_b: School buses have no tail swing
choice_c: Up to six inches
choice_d: Up to three feet
explanation: A school bus can have up to a three-foot tail swing, so the driver needs to check mirrors before and during any turning movements to monitor it.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.7.4, Tail Swing

question: Why can strong winds be especially hazardous to a school bus?
choice_a: Wind is only a concern for empty buses
choice_b: The side of a school bus acts like a sail on a sailboat, and strong winds can push it sideways, off the road, or tip it over
choice_c: School buses are unusually low to the ground and unaffected by wind
choice_d: Wind primarily affects fuel economy, not handling
explanation: Strong winds affect the handling of the school bus because the side of the bus acts like a sail on a sailboat; strong winds can push the bus sideways, move it off the road, or in extreme conditions, tip it over.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.7.2, Driving in High Winds

question: Is backing a school bus generally encouraged or discouraged, and when may a driver back the bus?
choice_a: Backing is encouraged as the safest maneuver in tight spaces
choice_b: Backing is strongly discouraged; a driver should back the bus only when there is no other safe way to move the vehicle, and never with students outside the bus
choice_c: Backing is only prohibited if students are still on the bus
choice_d: There is no restriction on backing a school bus
explanation: Backing a school bus is strongly discouraged; a driver should back only when there is no other safe way to move the vehicle, and should never back a school bus when students are outside of the bus.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.7.3, Backing

question: When backing a school bus with a lookout posted, what is the lookout's role?
choice_a: Lookouts are not permitted during backing maneuvers
choice_b: To warn the driver about obstacles, approaching persons, and other vehicles, but not to give directions on how to back the bus
choice_c: To operate the parking brake from outside the bus
choice_d: To physically direct the steering of the bus using hand signals
explanation: The purpose of the lookout is to warn the driver about obstacles, approaching persons, and other vehicles; the lookout should not give directions on how to back the bus.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.7.3, Backing

question: When should the roof-mounted white strobe lights on an equipped school bus be used?
choice_a: Only at railroad crossings
choice_b: Continuously, at all times while the bus is in motion
choice_c: Only during loading and unloading at school
choice_d: When the driver has limited visibility and cannot easily see around the bus
explanation: The overhead strobe light should be used when the driver has limited visibility, meaning they cannot easily see around the bus in front, behind, or beside it, subject to state or local regulations.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version) -- Section 10.7.1, Strobe Lights
